source.title: Revenge of Monosemanticity: Neuron Specialization as a New Form of Feature Learning in MLPs
source.authors: Amirhesam Abedsoltan; Enric Boix-Adserà; Fivos Kalogiannis; M. Belkin

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present; no apparent garbling or truncation.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures neuron specialization and cluster-selective activation in synthetic MLPs, but does not test or rely on superposition as defined in the claim. It does not study sparse features competing for dimensions, feature overlap or interference, or SAE feature recovery.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on neuron weight alignment and activation selectivity, which are related but distinct from superposition and the claim versions. Those results are recorded with versions ["none"]. It does not test whether sparse overcomplete features are stored as overlapping directions, whether polysemanticity results from limited capacity, or whether SAE features are canonical units.
record.test_reason: The study measures cluster-specific weight alignment (specialization) and cluster-selective firing (its 'monosemanticity' score) in one-hidden-layer synthetic regression MLPs. It does not test superposition or any version of the claim. The study's 'features' are Gaussian-mixture clusters and their predictive directions, not sparse features outnumbering dimensions. Width (4096) far exceeds the number of clusters (25 or 50), so capacity is never varied. No overlap or interference geometry, sparsity transition, LLM or SAE analysis, or feature dimensionality is measured. The interpretability literature on mono- and polysemanticity is cited only as context.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that MLPs on clustered data learn many local low-dimensional representations through neuron specialization, often with cluster-selective (monosemantic) firing, rather than one global representation. They also prove two results. Under small initialization, ReLU neurons specialize to a single cluster's span (Theorem 1). MLPs reach consistency with poly(K) samples, whereas rotationally invariant kernels and RFM with ground-truth AGOP do not (Theorem 2). Empirically, gated activations (ReGLU/SwiGLU) improve sample efficiency.
record.recipe_differences: The study does not reproduce or apply the Toy Models of Superposition method; it studies cluster-specific neuron specialization in synthetic regression MLPs.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported specialization and monosemanticity rates vary substantially across activation types and experiment settings.

fits_no_version.finding: In synthetic clustered regression, a substantial fraction of active MLP neurons align with one cluster's mean-plus-predictive span, well above a random-orientation null. Many of these neurons concentrate activation energy on that cluster. Rates vary strongly by activation (e.g. ReLU 15.71% vs GELU 77.66% specialized in Table 1). Specialization does not guarantee cluster-exclusive firing (GELU: 45.74% of specialized neurons have Mj > 1/2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Standard MLPs trained on clustered single- or multi-index regression learn neurons specialized and often selective to individual clusters, without explicit routing. The degree depends on activation and setup.

record.problems: Evidence is from synthetic clustered regression tasks and three runs per setting. The specialization and monosemanticity measurements concern cluster subspaces and activation energy, not overlapping feature representations or superposition.
record.rows_left_out: No results were omitted from the specialization and monosemanticity tables. Other sample-complexity and learned-gating results were not recorded because they do not measure the claim's feature-overlap or capacity constructs.

untested.parts: Features exceeding dimensions, nearly orthogonal overlapping storage, interference, sparsity-dependent phase transition, regular geometry.
Whether polysemanticity follows from features competing for limited capacity; dedicated vs shared dimensions by importance. Capacity is never constrained or varied.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise without capacity pressure. The setting has ample width and some non-monosemantic neurons, but polysemanticity and its causes are not analysed.
Distributed features or SAE-recoverable sparse features in LLMs.
Completeness, stability or canonicity of SAE features.
One-dimensional vs multi-dimensional superposed features. The multi-index experiment uses 3-D predictive spans per cluster but does not test superposition.

record.verdict_notes: The paper's use of 'monosemanticity' means cluster-selective activation energy among weight-aligned neurons, not the absence of superposed features. The rows are correctly linked to 'none'. One could argue a loose bearing on V3: some neurons are not cluster-selective despite ample width (4096 units for 25–50 clusters). However, the paper does not measure or interpret polysemanticity, so no verdict is given. Table 6 (random-orientation null, also at the Sj ≥ 0.7 threshold) and the sample-complexity figures are not needed for any version.

versions.untested_parts: Sparse features exceeding dimensionality, overlapping nearly orthogonal storage, interference, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether feature competition for limited capacity causes polysemantic neurons, or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions while others share.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise for reasons other than capacity pressure, and whether they are evidence for superposition.
Feature spreading across neurons or sparse-feature recovery in LLMs.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
Whether superposed features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional features.
